title: Two Brains Are Better Than One: Building a Faster, Cheaper Triage Agent with UiPath and Jev
body_markdown:
*How a “System 1 / System 2” pattern cut the cost of routing decisions in a UiPath coded agent to a fraction of a cent—and when the second brain still needs to be a human.*


Simple use case for using System One decisions with UiPath Coded Agents.


### The problem with using an LLM for everything


If you’ve built an agent in the last two years, you’ve probably done this: a ticket, an email, or a form comes in, and step one is “ask the LLM what this is.” Is it billing or technical? Is the customer angry? Should a human see this?


It works. It’s also overkill. You’re spending a full language-model call—hundreds of milliseconds to a few seconds, real tokens, real dollars — to answer a question that has three possible answers. Most of what an LLM does when you ask it “which department does this belong to?” is *not* reasoning. It’s committing to a decision it could have made almost instantly if it didn’t have to generate a sentence to get there.


Psychologists have a name for the split we’re dancing around here:[Daniel Kahneman’s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thinking,_Fast_and_Slow) System 1 and System 2. System 1 is fast, cheap, intuitive—the part of your brain that recognizes a friend’s face or knows a stove is hot without deliberating. System 2 is slow, effortful, and reserved for the problems that actually need it.


Most agent pipelines only have System 2. Every decision, however small, gets routed through the same expensive, deliberate machinery. This post is about giving an agent a System 1.


### Enter Jev


[TypeSafe AI](https://typesafe.ai/) recently introduced a category of model they call **System One models** , and their first is **Jev** . It’s a genuinely different shape of model: instead of generating text token by token, Jev takes a piece of state—a ticket, a transcript, a JSON blob, whatever—plus a set of *typed questions* , and returns calibrated, typed answers in a single pass.


Three primitives cover a surprising amount of ground:


- **Noul:** a yes/no question, answered as a probability from 0 to 1
- **Choice:** pick one label from a set, with a confidence and a full probability distribution
- **Score:** rate something against an ordered rubric (think a 0–2 “how upset is this customer” scale)


No prompt engineering. No parsing a model’s prose to extract a verdict. You ask a typed question, you get a typed answer, and it comes back in roughly the time it takes to blink—see the measured numbers below.


Jev vs LLM: latency measurements (log-scale)


### Building it into a UiPath agent


We built a small but complete example of this pattern into the[UiPath Python SDK’s samples](https://github.com/UiPath/uipath-python/tree/main/packages/uipath/samples/ticket-triage-agent) : a support-ticket triage agent that uses Jev as its System 1 and hands off to two different System 2s depending on what it finds.


The shape of it is simple:


```text
@traced()  def triage_ticket(ticket: TicketInput) -> TriageDecision:      """Run the fast Tier 1 structured triage over the ticket."""      client = TypeSafeClient()      response = client.system_one(          state={"subject": ticket.subject, "message": ticket.message},          questions={              "department": Choice(                  instructions="Which team should handle this ticket?",                  criteria={                      "billing": "Payments, invoicing, refunds, subscriptions",                      "technical": "Bugs, outages, integrations, errors",                      "sales": "Pricing, upgrades, new accounts, demos",                  },              ),              "is_urgent": Noul(instructions="Does this convey urgency?"),              "frustration": Score(                  instructions="How frustrated does the customer sound?",                  criteria=["Calm", "Frustrated", "Very angry"],              ),          },      )      ...
```


That call is the entire first tier. No system prompt to tune, no few-shot examples, no worrying about the model padding its answer with “Sure, I’d be happy to help you classify this ticket!” before finally telling you it’s billing.


From there, the agent branches:


```text
def needs_escalation(triage: TriageDecision) -> bool:      """Decide whether the ticket should go to a human instead of auto-reply."""      return (          triage.urgency >= URGENCY_THRESHOLD          or (triage.frustration_score / triage.frustration_scale) >= FRUSTRATION_THRESHOLD_FRACTION          or triage.department_confidence < ROUTING_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD      )
```


- **High urgency, high frustration, or a routing decision Jev isn’t confident about** → the ticket goes to a real human, via a UiPath **Action Center** QuickForm task, with Jev’s structured decision attached as context so the reviewer isn’t starting from a blank page.
- **Everything else** → the ticket goes to a real **LLM** , through UiPath’s LLM Gateway, with a department-specific system prompt that drafts a reply.


Notice what’s *not* happening in the common case: no human was interrupted, and the expensive model was only invoked to do the one thing it’s actually good at—writing a considered, well-phrased response—instead of also being asked to do triage on the side.


That’s the whole idea. System 1 handles volume. System 2—human or LLM—handles judgment.


### Watching it run


Here’s what a genuinely urgent ticket looks like going through the pipeline end to end, against a live UiPath tenant:


```text
HTTP Request: POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone "HTTP/1.1 200 OK"   (168ms)  HTTP Request: POST .../orchestrator_/tasks/GenericTasks/CreateTask "HTTP/1.1 201 Created"   output  ├── triage  │   ├── department: technical  │   ├── department_confidence: 1.0  │   ├── urgency: 0.99  │   ├── frustration_score: 1.85  │   └── frustration_scale: 2  ├── escalated: True  ├── auto_reply: None  └── action_task_id: 101634841  ✓ Successful execution.
```


Jev answered in under 200 milliseconds, correctly flagged both the urgency and the frustration, and the agent skipped straight to creating a real Action Center task—no LLM call, no waiting, no ambiguity about why it escalated. The reviewer opening that task sees exactly what Jev saw and exactly why the agent didn’t try to handle it alone.


### How much faster, actually?


“Faster and cheaper” is easy to claim and rarely quantified. So we measured it: same ticket, same target output shape (department / urgency / frustration), fired 10 times in parallel at each candidate, through the real, live APIs.


Jev vs LLM: latency measurements


Jev came back **13–23x faster at p50, 16–32x at p99** than two models that are themselves marketed as the fast, cheap end of their respective lineups—not against a slow flagship model, against the baseline everyone already reaches for when they want speed.


None of this makes the LLM path pointless—the point was never to make Jev write the reply. It’s that the *routing decision itself* doesn’t need a model an order of magnitude more expensive than the work it’s gating.


### Why this matters beyond one sample


The specific pairing here—Jev plus UiPath—is almost beside the point. The pattern generalizes to anywhere an agent currently burns an LLM call on a decision that’s really just a classification, a threshold, or a confidence check:


- Routing a document to the right extraction pipeline before a heavier OCR/LLM step runs
- Scoring queue items for priority before a robot picks them up
- Deciding whether a guardrail needs to escalate, or whether it’s safe to proceed
- Gating *any* multi-agent handoff on a fast, typed pre-check instead of a second full agent invocation


Anywhere you’re currently asking an LLM “which one is it?” and throwing away everything except its final word, there’s a good chance a System 1 model would answer faster, cheaper, and with a probability you can actually threshold on—leaving your System 2, human or machine, free to do the part of the job that deserves the attention.


**Try it yourself:** the full sample—mock-free, running against the real Jev API—lives at[packages/uipath/samples/ticket-triage-agent in the UiPath Python SDK repo](https://github.com/UiPath/uipath-python/tree/main/packages/uipath/samples/ticket-triage-agent) , complete with an evaluation set covering both the escalation and auto-reply paths across three departments.
